questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: choose the form of address that fits a first meeting with a complete stranger
questions.stem: At a community centre a volunteer offers to show a newcomer around the building. Which opening suits a first meeting with a stranger in that setting?

options.text: Guten Tag, mein Name ist Nora Feld, und ich wohne seit zwei Wochen in der Nähe.
Moin, ich bin Nora, und ich wähle jedenfalls erst mal das Sie, oder?
options.misconception: uses a casual northern greeting and then puts the choice of register on the addressee

options.text: Guten Tag, ich bin Nora Feld, und ich wünsche Ihnen einen angenehmen Aufenthalt.
options.misconception: speaks a formula that belongs to staff seeing a guest off, not to a newcomer introducing herself

options.text: Tach, ich bin neu hier, freut mich, und ihr seid alle ganz schön lange da, was?
options.misconception: treats one unknown volunteer as a familiar group with a plural du and a casual street opening

questions.explanation: German picks the form of address from the distance between the speakers, not from how friendly the moment feels. Sie is the default with adults a speaker does not know, which is exactly the case at a community centre where a volunteer is in charge and the visitor has no shared ground, whereas du is used with friends, family, children and colleagues only after the more powerful person has offered it. The capital letter marks Sie as the polite form, and it governs the inflected verb, so the same sentence gives Sie wünschen against du wünschst. The second option fails twice, because Moin belongs to a relaxed northern register and because the trailing oder? hands the decision about register to a stranger. The third is grammatically sound but pragmatically wrong, since ein angenehmer Aufenthalt is what a receptionist wishes a departing guest. The fourth addresses a group informally to a single person who has given no such permission.
questions.hint: Ask who holds the position in this room and whether the two have any shared history.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: attach a German greeting to the hour at which it is said
questions.stem: A receptionist greets a visitor at half past nine in the morning. Which greeting does that hour call for?

options.text: Guten Morgen, Frau Kaya.
Guten Abend, Frau Kaya.
options.misconception: uses the evening greeting in the morning because both words are equally polite

options.text: Gute Nacht, Frau Kaya.
options.misconception: uses the parting formula for the night at a desk in the morning

options.text: Guten Tag, Frau Kaya.
options.misconception: picks the all-day greeting as though it named the morning in particular

questions.explanation: German has no single greeting for the whole day, and the choice tracks the hour. Guten Morgen covers roughly from dawn until noon, Guten Tag runs from early afternoon until dusk, Guten Abend from late afternoon until going to bed, and Gute Nacht belongs to parting at night or to a late phone call. Half past nine in the morning therefore falls squarely in the first window, and a receptionist who is being professional uses the time-specific word rather than the general one. Guten Tag is not wrong in the abstract, which is why it is the tempting distractor, but it gives the visitor no sense of how early the day already is, and treating it as a morning-only greeting is what the option claims. Guten Abend and Gute Nacht both shift the meeting to the wrong part of the day, and the latter normally closes an encounter rather than opening one.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the day the hour named in the question falls into.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Farewell and the formality of the relationship
questions.learningObjective: choose a farewell that matches the rank and familiarity of the addressee
questions.stem: A candidate thanks a company director at the door after a job interview. Which farewell matches that relationship and that setting?

options.text: Vielen Dank für das Gespräch. Auf Wiedersehen.
Tschüss, bis bald, und drück mir die Daumen.
options.misconception: uses a school-leaver farewell and asks a senior figure for a personal thumbs-up

options.text: Gute Nacht, und danke für den Kaffee.
options.misconception: wishes good night at a door in the early evening instead of closing a meeting

options.text: Bis gleich, ich melde mich dann.
options.misconception: assumes the two will meet again within minutes when the meeting is already over

questions.explanation: The level of formality in a German farewell is fixed by the relationship, and a job interview leaves both parties in the Sie register for the whole encounter, including the parting. Auf Wiedersehen is the neutral-lehrhaft und korrekt choice for that, and the preceding Vielen Dank für das Gespräch does the thanking the way a candidate can. Tschüss belongs to friends and peers, and drück mir die Daumen asks the director to take a personal interest, which no applicant should do in a first encounter. Gute Nacht presupposes that the day is over and that the speaker is going to bed, so it can be out of place at four in the afternoon. Bis gleich promises a meeting within minutes, which nothing in the situation supports. The test is simple: if the two have not arranged to meet again, the farewell must not claim that they have.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two people have already agreed to see each other again.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: build a wh-question in which the question word takes the subject slot
questions.stem: A new colleague wants to know where a visitor comes from without sounding nosy. Which question is built the way German builds it?

options.text: Woher kommen Sie, Frau Öztürk?
Woher Sie kommen?
options.misconception: puts the subject ahead of the verb, which is the order of a statement rather than of a question

options.text: Sie kommen woher?
options.misconception: leaves the conjugated verb out and expects the question word alone to carry the clause

options.text: Woher sind Sie kommen?
options.misconception: keeps a full verb in the infinitive slot after the copula, which German does not allow

questions.explanation: A wh-question in German uses the same three slots as any other clause: the question word takes the slot that a fronted element would take, the conjugated verb moves up to second position, and the subject follows it. So Woher comes from the verb of coming and takes the fronted slot, kommen is the conjugated verb and so takes the second position, and Sie lands behind it. The subject-first variant in option B is a declarative order and turns the question into a remark the addressee has to correct. Option C drops the finite verb altogether, which no German question can do even in the shortest register. Option D shows the error that prepositions and separable prefixes encourage: German finite verbs never stand in a slot after a modal or copula in an infinitive construction, so Sie sind gekommen would be needed for a past form and you cannot keep kommen in the infinitive slot there. The politeness comes from the Sie form and the surname, not from any extra word.
questions.hint: Mark the finite verb first, then slot the subject after it, and see whether the question still reads.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: place the conjugated verb in first position to form a yes-or-no question
questions.stem: A receptionist needs to know whether a visitor has an appointment at all. Which of these is a correctly built yes-or-no question?

options.text: Haben Sie einen Termin?
Sie haben einen Termin?
options.misconception: keeps the subject in front, which is the order of a statement and not of a question

options.text: Haben einen Termin Sie?
options.misconception: leaves the subject out and hopes the auxiliary carries the whole question

options.text: Haben Sie einen Termin, oder?
options.misconception: adds a disjunction marker that a plain yes-or-no question does not need

questions.explanation: German forms a yes-or-no question by sending the conjugated verb to the front and pushing the subject behind it, which is the visible sign that the same three words can be read either way. Haben Sie einen Termin is that order, and the question mark alone settles that no answer is expected in the form of a sentence. The second option is the declarative order, so the addressee first has to decide whether it is a statement and only then notice the mark, which is exactly the hesitation a learner should avoid provoking. The third breaks the pairing of verb and subject, which German never separates. The fourth is worth knowing about but is not what a receptionist would say to establish the fact; it is used when the speaker already suspects one alternative and wants the other named. A learner who wants to be safe with oder is not wrong, only more verbose than the situation needs.
questions.hint: Locate the conjugated verb and ask whether it is the first word of the clause.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: keep a fronted question word and its preposition together in front of the noun
questions.stem: A visitor wants to know in which city a stranger lives. Which question keeps the preposition and the noun it governs together?

options.text: In welcher Stadt wohnen Sie?
Wo wohnen Sie in welcher Stadt?
options.misconception: sets up two question words in one clause, which German avoids

options.text: In welcher Stadt Sie wohnen?
options.misconception: slots the subject between the question phrase and the conjugated verb

options.text: Sie wohnen in welcher Stadt?
options.misconception: leaves the question word stranded at the end, where it can no longer govern its noun

questions.explanation: A German wh-question has one question phrase, and when that phrase begins with a preposition the preposition travels with its noun to the very front: in welcher Stadt occupies the first slot, wohnen takes the second, and Sie comes last. Option B is wrong because German does not build the second question phrase into a second question word; the interrogative slot holds one element. Option C keeps the fronted phrase but breaks the verb-second rule of the subordinate-like question frame, so a reader has to guess where the verb belongs. Option D is the commonest learner version, because English allows you to say which city do you live in, but in German a stranded question word at the end can no longer stand in front of the noun it belongs to, and the noun then looks unaccounted for. Note that such a question is only possible without a preposition, as in Welche Stadt wohnen Sie, and even there it is marked.
questions.hint: Decide whether the question word can still stand in front of its noun in the order you have written.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Referring to people in an official note
questions.learningObjective: read what a form of reference and a pronoun tell you about the relationship between the people named
questions.stem: A staff member writes at the top of a circular: 'Frau Bauer, ich darf Ihnen Herrn Keller vorstellen, unseren neuen Kollegen aus der IT-Abteilung.' What do the form Herrn and the pronoun Ihnen tell the reader?

options.text: That the note is written in the polite register throughout, and Herrn is the inflected form a man takes in a phrase with an article
That Herrn shows respect for the woman, who is named in the very same sentence
options.misconception: reads the inflected form of Herr as a courtesy aimed at the woman standing next to him

options.text: That Herrn is the way a speaker addresses the man directly, and the note is therefore quoting live speech
options.misconception: confuses the article form used when a man is mentioned with the form of direct address

options.text: That the two colleagues are on first-name terms, and Herrn is only a courtesy put in writing
options.misconception: reads a polite written note as evidence that the writer and the people named address each other with du

questions.explanation: Two separate signals are at work. Ihnen is the dative of the polite Sie, and a dative pronoun in a subordinate object slot tells the reader that the whole note is written with Sie, so Frau Bauer is an addressee the writer does not yet know personally or does not treat as a friend. Herrn is the accusative singular of Herr and appears because the man is being mentioned with an article in an object phrase, where the masculine definite article fuses with the noun. The same spelling also serves as the direct address, so the form alone does not prove which function it has here; the phrase position does, and here it follows vorstellen, which takes an accusative object. The distractors each swap a grammatical signal for a social guess: politeness shown by Herrn rather than by the pronoun, a courtesy taken to be aimed at the wrong person, or a written Sie read as licence to use du.
questions.hint: Find the case the phrase sits in and ask which pronoun carries the politeness.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: place a polite table order with a modal of wish and the particle bitte
questions.stem: A guest at a beer garden wants to order without sounding abrupt. Which phrase sounds like a normal table order there?

options.text: Ich hätte gern ein Weißbier, bitte.
Ich will sofort ein Weißbier geben.
options.misconception: uses a bare verb of volition with an object, which reads as a demand rather than an order

options.text: Ich essen gern ein Weißbier, bitte.
options.misconception: sends the infinitive to the front, which German only allows once a modal has been dropped

options.text: Ich habe gern ein Weißbier, bitte.
options.misconception: swaps the verb of liking for a verb of possession, so the order sounds like a claim on a thing

questions.explanation: The ordinary German table order is a wish dressed as a statement: hätte is the second subjunctive of haben, which puts the speaker one step away from the act, gern adds the preference, and bitte carries the politeness that Ich möchte would otherwise have to do. Together they produce an order the waiter can act on without the guest having issued a command. Option B is a demand, since wollen with a bare object tells the waiter what to do rather than what the guest would like, and the extra sofort makes it worse. Option C fails on word order: essen in the infinitive can only open a clause if a governing modal such as möchte or werde has been left out, and here nothing has. Option D replaces the verb of liking with haben, which claims the guest already owns a beer, a reading a waiter might act on quite differently. The particle bitte is optional but common, and it belongs after the verb, not before the subject.
questions.hint: Look for a verb that puts the order at one remove from the speaker's own act.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: ask for the price of a named article in idiomatic German
questions.stem: A customer sees a coat in a shop window with a price card and wants to know the cost. Which question is idiomatic?

options.text: Was kostet der Mantel?
Was ist der Mantel?
options.misconception: asks what a thing is rather than what it costs, which is how the question is built in English

options.text: Was für ein Mantel ist das?
options.misconception: sets up a type question in statement order, so the price is never requested

options.text: Wie viel ist der Mantel?
options.misconception: offers a measure word where a bare price takes none

questions.explanation: German asks what a thing costs with a full verb, so the price question is Was kostet der Mantel, and the cost is then given in euros. The near neighbour Was ist der Mantel asks about the object or the identity of the thing, so a learner who copies that frame from English gets a question about the coat rather than its price. Option C is a type question, and it is in the wrong order besides, since Was für ein Mantel belongs in a slot a speaker can build with the verb at the end. Option D is the tempting one because German does use Wie viel for quantities, but a price is a bare number, so Wie viel is either incomplete or shifts the question to a weight or a length. The stem in the question word, so a learned form worth keeping is Wie viel kostet der Mantel, which is also correct and puts the price in the same frame.
questions.hint: Check whether the verb asks about value, about cost, or about a measure.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Quantities and containers in a restaurant
questions.learningObjective: match a container noun to the quantity of water ordered for a table
questions.stem: A group at a restaurant orders water for the whole table rather than for one person. Which phrase names that quantity?

options.text: Eine Kanne Wasser, bitte
Ein Glas Wasser, bitte
options.misconception: names the small drinking vessel rather than the jug filled for the table

options.text: Eine Flasche Bier, bitte
options.misconception: names the container a drink is sold in, which a restaurant table rarely fills

options.text: Ein Becher Kaffee, bitte
options.misconception: names the takeaway cup, so the order reads as something for the journey

questions.explanation: A Kanne is the jug a restaurant fills for a table, and it is the unit German uses for that amount, so Eine Kanne Wasser, bitte is the order a group places. A Glas is the small drinking vessel one person takes at the table, which is why the second option describes a different quantity rather than a different word for the same one. A Flasche names the container a drink is sold in and is common on a list, but it is not what a table is served, and the option also changes the drink, so it fails twice. A Becher is the takeaway cup, which points to a different situation entirely. Worth noticing that German puts no number after eine when the container itself carries the measure, so there is no ein Liter in front of it; adding a number would double the count.
questions.hint: Ask which vessel a waiter would carry to the table rather than to the door.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Describing a dish with an adjective
questions.learningObjective: place an adjective in the predicate slot without an ending
questions.stem: A cook tastes a soup, finds nothing wrong with it, and wants to say so without naming anybody else as the source. Which sentence is right?

options.text: Die Suppe schmeckt gut.
Die Suppe ist leckere.
options.misconception: carries the ending of the attributive form into a predicate, where the adjective has none

options.text: Die Suppe schmeckt leckere.
options.misconception: makes the predicate slot take an inflected adjective, which only happens before a noun

options.text: Die Suppe ist ein leckere Essen.
options.misconception: gives a neuter noun the feminine ending that a feminine article would require

questions.explanation: An adjective that stands alone in the predicate has no ending, and the verb of tasting is a neat way of saying so because it names the dish as the one doing the pleasing. Die Suppe schmeckt gut therefore needs no ending on gut at all. The error in option B is the classic one: leckere is the form that comes before a noun, as in eine leckere Suppe, and dropping the noun behind it leaves an ending with nothing to agree with. Option C makes the same mistake and adds a second one, because schmeckt is transitive here and the direct object is already the subject of the sentence, so the slot after it is for a bare predicate, not for an adjective that expects a noun. Option D shows the opposite slip, treating the neuter Essen as though it were feminine, and ein is one of the three articles that never changes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the adjective has a noun directly in front of it or is standing on its own.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: mark a restriction as a negative of the verb of eating and keep the prepositional phrase free of articles
questions.stem: A guest reads a menu that lists a soup made with cream and needs the waiter to have the one fact straight. Which sentence states the restriction correctly and asks for the right dish?

options.text: Ich vertrage keine Sahne, deshalb brauche ich eine Suppe ohne Sahne.
Ich vertrage keine Sahne, deshalb brauche ich eine Suppe ohne eine Sahne.
options.misconception: keeps an article in front of a mass noun, which German does not use after ohne

options.text: Ich vertrage keine Sahne, deshalb brauche ich eine ohne Sahne Suppe.
options.misconception: leaves an adjective plus noun stranded between two articles, so the phrase is no longer well formed

options.text: Ich vertrage keine Sahne, deshalb brauche ich eine Suppe mit keine Sahne.
options.misconception: puts a negative adjective behind a preposition that would need the dative, which takes kein in the dative too

questions.explanation: The first clause uses the verb of tolerating with a negated noun in the accusative, which is the normal way a German speaker states a food restriction, and the second clause names the dish and the missing ingredient. The second option fails because Sahne is a mass noun, and after ohne such nouns appear without an article; the phrase would read as the absence of one portion rather than of the ingredient. The third option puts the noun after its own modifier and between two articles, and German requires attributive modifiers to stand in the determiner slot immediately before the noun, so eine ohne Sahne Suppe is not well formed. The fourth option reaches for mit and then keeps a nominative-looking negative, when a negated phrase after a preposition takes the dative form of kein. In each case the guest's intention is clear to a waiter, which is why the slips survive in speech, but they are errors on paper.
questions.hint: Check the article slot after ohne, and check the case a negative needs after a preposition.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: What makes a German request polite
questions.learningObjective: name the grammatical and lexical devices that put distance into a request
questions.stem: A pupil asks a teacher for a few extra days in the middle of a lesson. Why does 'Könnten Sie mir bitte bis Freitag ein paar Tage schenken?' sound civilised while 'Gib mir bis Freitag Tage' does not?

answer.exemplar: Politeness in German is built from four separate devices, and the two sentences differ in three of them at once. The first uses Könnten, the second subjunctive of können, which turns an ability the pupil certainly has into something hypothetical and so pushes the request one step away from the speaker's own act. The second uses bitte, a particle that can stand after the conjugated verb and carries the politeness the word order has not supplied. The third is the dative pronoun mir, because a request is directed at somebody, and the dative of a person is the normal object of a verb of giving such as schenken. The fourth is the plural pronoun Sie, which keeps the register formal without naming the addressee. The bare sentence keeps none of this: Gib is the familiar imperative, mir is right but naked, and the singular du is not available between a pupil and a teacher. The unfilled time slot also matters, because bis Freitag needs a verb phrase after it, which is what schenken provides.

questions.explanation: German marks distance rather than adding empty politeness words, and that is why a single feature can change the character of a request. A verb in the second subjunctive or in the würde form reports what the speaker could do rather than asserting what they are doing, which puts the action and the person asking it at different levels, and it is the level that a pupil, a tenant or a candidate can afford. The particle bitte is a separate device: it takes no object, it can move about inside the clause, and it adds nothing that could not be left out, so its presence is pure politeness. The dative slot is a grammatical fact rather than a courtesy, since a request is directed at a person, and the pronoun Sie supplies the register. Read the two sentences feature by feature and the difference is measurable, which is what makes it teachable rather than a matter of taste.
questions.hint: List what each sentence does with the verb, the particle, the pronoun and the register.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: separate well-formed polite requests from forms a learner commonly produces
questions.stem: A tenant wants a landlord to help with a move. Which of these five sentences are well-formed German requests?

options.text: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?
Können Sie mir bitte helfen?
Sie können mir bitte helfen?
options.misconception: puts the subject in front of the modal, which is the order of a statement rather than of a question

options.text: Können Sie mir bitte zu helfen?
options.misconception: adds a zu infinitive after können, which already contains the infinitive itself

options.text: Würden Sie mir bitte helfen?

questions.explanation: A modal in first position carries a question, so Können, Könnten and Würden all open a well-formed request, and in each case mir follows the pronoun Sie, bitte comes after the modal as the first piece of the non-finite area, and helfen closes the sentence as a bare infinitive. Option B uses the plain present of können and is still entirely normal with Sie, so a learner who thinks only the subjunctive can be polite is over-correcting. Option E uses the würde form of the same mood and is equally acceptable. Option C keeps the subject in front, which turns the modal into a claim about what the listener is able to do. Option D is the giveaway: a modal verb already stands in the finite slot, so there is no zu infinitive slot to fill.
questions.hint: Find the finite verb in each sentence and check whether anything sits between it and the subject.

questions.learningObjective: put the four parts of a German telephone opening in the order a caller says them
questions.stem: A caller reaches a company switchboard and wants to be put through to Frau Brandt. Put the four parts in the order the caller would say them.

options.text: Können Sie mich verbinden?
options.misconception: asks the operator to connect before saying who is calling, which is not how a German caller opens

options.text: Eine Sekunde, ich stelle Sie durch.
options.misconception: puts the operator's own line into first position, when it comes last in the call

options.misconception: leaves out the name and the firm, so the operator has nothing to connect

The addressee comes second, since naming the person wanted is the point of the call. The request follows, with the verb in the second position of the question and mir as the dative object of verbinden. The operator's reply comes last, because it answers the request. Option A inverts the first two moves, and an operator who has not been told who is calling cannot act on it. Option B belongs to the operator and cannot be the caller's first move. questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Recasting an informal note for an office
questions.learningObjective: raise the register of a request while keeping what is being asked unchanged
questions.stem: A friend has written 'Hey, kannst du mir kurz den Termin schicken? Danke dir!' Rewrite the request in a register that would be acceptable in a company office.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the note is informal throughout, and the markers are visible one by one. Hey is a casual English greeting rather than a German one, kannst du is the familiar modal with the familiar pronoun, the verb sits at the end of a question which is fine but not what the office uses, and Danke dir closes with the informal particle attached to the pronoun. Stage two: 'Könnten Sie mir bitte den Termin kurz zusenden? Vielen Dank im Voraus.' is the expected version. The greeting goes entirely, the pronoun becomes Sie, kannst becomes the second subjunctive Könnten, which adds a degree of distance, bitte is inserted after the modal, schicken becomes the more formal Zusenden in an office note, and the thanks becomes the fixed phrase Vielen Dank im Voraus, which asks for the trouble in advance. What must not change is the content: a request for the appointment, sent soon, with thanks. Anything that turned the request into a demand, dropped the thanks, or added an excuse would no longer be the same note.

questions.explanation: A register change is a controlled operation, and the discipline lies in changing one thing at a time. The informal note carries four separable markers: an English greeting, the familiar modal, the familiar pronoun and a thanks that ends with a particle attached to that pronoun. Each has a formal counterpart that does the same work, which is why the rewrite can be done without rewriting the request itself. The verb of sending also has a more formal member, zusenden, and an office reader will expect it, though it is a matter of convention rather than grammar. What makes the exercise useful is the negative test: after the rewrite, the note must still ask for the same thing, still say it is needed soon, and still thank the reader. A version that adds an excuse, or drops the thanks, or arrives earlier, has changed the message rather than its clothing.
questions.hint: Mark the four informal markers first, then replace one at a time and check that the request itself has not moved.

questions.learningObjective: build a checking question that repeats what was said with the modal verb of understanding
questions.stem: A speaker has just explained a return procedure, and a listener wants to check the one detail that will matter at the post office. Which sentence does that job properly?

options.text: Habe ich Sie richtig verstanden, dass ich das Formular per Post schicke?
Habe ich das Formular richtig verstanden, dass ich es per Post schicke?
options.misconception: makes the object the thing understood, so the question is about the form rather than the instruction

options.text: Habe ich Sie richtig verstanden, ob ich das Formular per Post schicke?
options.misconception: uses ob, which asks for information instead of checking a statement already made

options.text: Habe ich richtig verstanden Sie, dass ich das Formular per Post schicke?

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: What a complete German apology contains
questions.learningObjective: set out the four parts of a German apology and identify what is not required
questions.stem: A colleague is annoyed after a project slipped by a week. What has to be in a complete German apology, and what does a complete one not need?

answer.exemplar: A complete German apology has four parts. It names the act, in the first person and in the perfect, as in Es tut mir leid, dass ich die Frist nicht gehalten habe, where the verb of regret takes the dative, the dass-clause carries the act, nicht sits in front of the noun inside that clause, and habe stands at the end. It then shows the effect on the other party in a subordinate clause: Ich weiß, dass euch das viel Arbeit gemacht hat. It states the change as a fact: Ich melde mich künftig früher. And it stops. What is not required is a reason. Es liegt nicht an mir, sondern an der Software offered before the regret reads as a defence, while the same sentence placed after the regret is harmless. Ich bitte um Verständnis is not required either, and because it is a formula it can never do the work of the first sentence. A passive is the other standard retreat, since der Termin wurde nicht eingehalten leaves nobody doing anything at all.

questions.explanation: A German apology is judged on four things and readers check them in order, which is why a formula alone is not enough. The act has to be named by the person responsible, the effect on the other party has to be acknowledged, the change has to be stated as a fact about the future rather than as a promise, and then the apology stops. What German readers are unusually sensitive about is a reason offered too early, because Es liegt nicht an mir and aber ich hatte keine Zeit both move the sentence from the act to the cause, and a reader who is still waiting for the act hears a defence. The useful test is to read the apology aloud and ask whether the first sentence names what the speaker did. If it does, the rest can be forgiven; if it does not, no amount of Ich bitte um Verständnis will help. Note too that the German of apology takes a dass-clause, unlike the English, so Es tut mir leid, dass es so kurzfristig kam is needed and Es tut mir leid zu hören is a different act.
questions.hint: Ask whether the first sentence names what the speaker did, and where the reason appears.

Sie ist eine zuverlässige Kollegin, die ihre Termine immer hält says what she is, die introduces the relative clause, and ihre Termine immer hält gives the evidence, with the conjugated verb at the end of the relative clause. A chain of adjectives with no article is not a description but a list, and a description of a place would use the same machinery, so nothing in the bare list distinguishes the two. questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Choosing the perfect or the simple past
questions.learningObjective: set out when German uses the perfect and when it uses the simple past
questions.stem: A learner asks when to write 'Ich habe gearbeitet' and when to write 'Ich arbeitete'. What actually decides the choice in German?

answer.exemplar: The choice is not about how far back the event is but about two things: whether the state or the result still matters, and whether the speaker is telling the story or reporting the fact. German uses the perfect for a past that is still relevant, for a stretch without a specific end, and for anything whose point is that it happened at all: Ich habe im Januar dort gearbeitet, Das habe ich nicht gewusst, Als Kind habe ich dort gewohnt. It uses the simple past for a stretch that is over and closed, for a narrative with a sequence of events, and for the modals in almost every register: Ich hatte keine Zeit, Ich wollte gehen, Ich musste warten. The verbs of having and of being are the practical test, because they carry the simple past forms hatte and war, and those are what a spoken account of a closed period uses. A learner who is unsure can replace the simple past with the perfect of the same verb in most contexts, and the reverse is not true, since swapping a perfect for a simple past can change what a sentence claims.

questions.explanation: The choice is not about how far back the event lies but about two things: whether the past state or result still matters, and whether the speaker is telling a story or filing a fact. That is why the confusion does not go away with more vocabulary. The perfect is the default in spoken German and covers anything whose present relevance is the point, which is most of what is said in conversation: Ich habe dort drei Jahre gearbeitet, Das habe ich nicht gewusst, Als Kind habe ich bei meiner Tante gewohnt. The simple past is required for the modals, is the usual form for the verbs of having and being, and is preferred for a stretch of time that is closed, which makes it the tense of an account: Damals hatte ich keine Zeit. A learner who is unsure has a safe move, because swapping a simple past for a perfect is possible in most contexts, while the reverse is not, since changing a perfect to a simple past can change what the sentence claims. The verb of being is the quickest check on a passage: a spoken account of a finished period will keep war, and a text full of bin gewesen reads like a list.
questions.hint: Ask whether the period is closed and whether the order of events matters.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The scale of German frequency adverbs
questions.learningObjective: place the common frequency adverbs on a scale and explain what the scale does not measure
questions.stem: A learner wants to place nie, selten, gelegentlich, oft, regelmäßig and immer in order. What does that order measure, and what does it leave out?

answer.exemplar: The German frequency adverbs form a scale that measures how often something happens: nie, selten, gelegentlich, oft, regelmäßig, immer, with ständig and dauernd at the top for something that never stops. Two things fall outside that scale. The first is regularity, which is a separate axis: jemand kann regelmäßig schwimmen und trotzdem selten ins Schwimmbad gehen, so a learner who sorts all seven words on one line will get this pair wrong. The second is a figure, and a figure is nearly always clearer: Ich spiele zweimal im Monat Klavier says more than Ich spiele regelmäßig Klavier and cannot be misunderstood. Two further habits are worth forming. To hedge about a single exception, use manchmal or ein- oder zweimal rather than gelegentlich. To say something has happened before, use schon or schon öfter, as in Das habe ich schon gesagt, where the adverb is about the past and not about a habit. And in the negative, nicht viel and nicht gern sit at a different point on the scale from nie, which says never at all.

questions.explanation: The order runs from nie through selten and gelegentlich to oft, regelmäßig and immer, and it measures one thing only: how many times something happens. Two things fall outside it, and both cause trouble. The first is regularity, which is a separate axis: someone can be regelmäßig at something and do it rarely, and someone can do something often in bursts at the end of a month. The second is a figure, which is usually clearer than any of the adverbs, so a speaker who says he plays twice a month has said something that cannot be misread, while regelmäßig leaves the listener guessing. A learner who wants to hedge should reach for manchmal when the point is a single exception, and for ab und zu when the frequency is low and the register informal. The adverbs also carry aspect, which matters more than it looks: schon öfter gesagt says the speaker has said it more than once before, which is a claim about the past rather than about a habit.
questions.hint: Ask whether the adverb answers how many times or whether there is a pattern.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Three ways to repair a spoken message
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the German strategies for misunderstanding, non-reception and self-correction
questions.stem: A listener has followed a spoken instruction badly. What do the three German repair strategies each repair, and why does a speaker need all three?

answer.exemplar: German has three repair moves and each one fixes a different failure. Rückfragen nach Verstehen covers a message that arrived but was not taken in, and the German form makes the detail a yes-or-no question, as in Sie meinen also, ich stehe am Landhausweg, which gives the speaker something to confirm. Die Bitte um Wiederholung covers a message that was not received at all, and the German form asks for the same words again rather than for a louder voice, as in Könnten Sie den Namen bitte noch einmal wiederholen. Die Korrektur in der Mitte covers a slip the speaker has noticed, and the German form is a short opener followed by the corrected noun, as in Ach so, ich meinte die Nebenstraße, nicht die Hauptstraße, which repairs without stopping the conversation. A learner who knows only one of the three will be stranded by the other two failures, and the choice depends on which of them has just happened rather than on style. The three differ in politeness as well, since a check for understanding can be very direct while a request for repetition has to be soft.

questions.explanation: German has three repair moves, and each one covers a different failure, which is why a speaker who knows only one of them gets stranded. A check for understanding covers a message that arrived but was not taken in, and the German form is to put the detail into a yes-or-no question, as in Sie meinen also, ich stehe am Landhausweg, because a question gives the original speaker something to confirm and a statement gives nothing. A request for repetition covers a message that was not received at all, and the German form asks for the same words again rather than for more volume, as in Könnten Sie den Namen bitte noch einmal wiederholen. A correction in the middle covers a slip the speaker has just noticed, and the German form is a short opener plus the corrected material, as in Ach so, ich meinte die Nebenstraße, nicht die Hauptstraße, which repairs without stopping. The three also differ in politeness, so a learner who picks the wrong one apologises to the wrong person.
questions.hint: Decide whether the message was not taken in, not heard, or said wrongly.

questions.topic: Recasting a report as a spoken account
questions.learningObjective: convert the written perfects of a short report into the simple pasts of a spoken account
questions.stem: A report reads 'Letzten Sommer bin ich nach Krakau gefahren. An der Unterkunft habe ich drei Nächte bezahlt. Die Altstadt war sehr schön.' Rewrite it as a spoken account in the simple past.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the text is written in the register of a report, and the two perfects mark that. Bin ich gefahren and habe ich bezahlt both use an auxiliary and a participle, which keeps each event in a list and leaves the reader to work out for itself whether one thing followed another. Stage two: 'Letzten Sommer fuhr ich nach Krakau. An der Unterkunft zahlte ich drei Nächte. Die Altstadt war wirklich schön.' is expected. The auxiliary disappears entirely, the participle disappears with it, and the three clauses now read in the order they happened, which is what a spoken account is. The word wirklich comes in because a person telling the story colours it, and a report would not. The one form that cannot change is war, since the simple past of the verb of being is already what the report used, and a learner who changes it to gewesen has left the genre rather than rewritten it. The content that must survive: last summer, Krakau, three nights, and a positive judgement about the old town.

questions.explanation: The rewrite is a change of genre and the grammar follows the genre, which is why it cannot be done by a rule of thumb about distance in time. In the report the perfect carries each fact at a distance: the auxiliary and the participle keep the events in a list, and nothing in them suggests that one thing happened before another. A spoken account is a sequence, and the simple past is the shape German uses for a sequence, so every auxiliary and every participle disappears and only the verb remains. One form resists the change and that is a useful check, since the simple past of the verb of being is the same shape and cannot be swapped for a perfect in a stretch of narration. What must not change is the content: the year, the destination, the number of nights and the judgement about the old town all survive untouched, and a rewrite that adds a reason or drops the opinion is no longer the same report.
